So you are applying for September. The thing nobody tells you is that the campus is the size of a small town, which changes how you plan a Tuesday.
That is the kind of detail I cannot get from a website. What was the part that surprised you most in the first term?
The workload, which is not difficult, only constant. Nothing in week one is hard. All of it at once is overwhelming.
And the people who drop out — is it because of the marks?
Almost never. Most of the students who leave are the ones nobody noticed, which is a much sadder sentence than the one about marks.
So the thing that actually matters is the support network, not the timetable.
Exactly, and it is not friends. My supervisor, who is impossible to find on a Monday, answers everything on a Thursday. That is the sort of thing a peer tells you and a handbook never does.
How long did it take you to settle in, honestly? And what would you do differently if you started again in September?

Every year we lose people in the first term, and the students who leave are almost never the students who are failing. I want to be very clear about that, because everybody assumes the opposite. The ones who go are the ones who have not spoken to anybody, and that is a completely different problem with a completely different solution. Now, international students in particular wait longer before they ask for help, and I understand why. Asking a question in a second language feels like admitting that you should not be here, and of course it is not that at all, but it feels like it in October when everybody around you seems to know where the room is. The delay is the risk. Not the language, the delay. So the one thing I ask of every new student, and I ask it in week one, is this. Speak to three people whose job it is to help you, before you have a problem. A supervisor, a peer mentor, somebody in this office. Five minutes each. Then the first real conversation you have with any of them is not an emergency, and I promise you that changes what happens in March.

The thing that made the difference for me was in the first week and it had nothing to do with my course. I joined a team, which put me in a room twice a week with people who were not studying what I was studying, and almost everybody I now rely on came out of that room. My classes gave me classmates. The team gave me a network, and I did not plan it that way. There are four people I ask for help now, and each one is for a different thing, which sounds calculated and is really just what happens when you stop expecting one person to be everything. Nobody can be your whole support network. They get tired, and then you have nothing. And if I were talking to somebody arriving in September, I would say two things. Six weeks is how long settling in takes, so do not judge the place or yourself before then. And the people who make the most of the first year are not the ones who arrive ready. They are the ones who ask early, while it is still a question and not yet a problem.
